aiOverview.content: The Integrated Public Alert & Warning System (IPAWS) is FEMA's national system that allows federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial authorities to send authenticated, life-saving emergency messages to the public. It simultaneously distributes alerts via mobile phones (Wireless Emergency Alerts), radio/television (Emergency Alert System), and NOAA Weather Radios. Key Aspects of IPAWS Alerts: Purpose: To protect life and property by providing localized, timely warnings (e.g., severe weather, missing persons, local emergencies). How it Works: Alerting authorities submit messages using the Common Alerting Protocol (CAP), which are then disseminated to multiple channels. No Sign-Up Needed: Alerts are sent automatically to cell phones in the targeted area; there is no need to sign up or opt-in. Types of Alerts: Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA): Text-like messages on mobile phones. Emergency Alert System (EAS): Alerts broadcast on TV and radio. NOAA Weather Radio: Messages for weather and non-weather events. Alerting Authorities: Authorized local officials, such as police or emergency management departments, can issue alerts, rather than relying solely on federal authority. Testing: IPAWS and WEA are tested regularly, including state-level tests, to ensure functionality. Components of IPAWS: IPAWS-OPEN: The open platform for emergency networks that validates and authenticates messages. Alerting Authorities: Organizations trained and accredited by FEMA to use the system. Alerting Pathways: The communication infrastructure, including cellular carriers, radio, and television stations. For more information, individuals can visit Ready.gov/alerts. Ready.gov/alerts

references.title: Folks, there seems to be some confusion about weather alerts on our smartphones, and who should receive what alerts. Please read on for some info and resources. The only *official* alerts (i.e. direct from a government source) that we control that you would get on your phone are called Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEAs). They will be issued for any Tornado Warnings, as well as for high-end (REALLY serious) severe thunderstorms, flash floods, and snow squalls. WEA will not activate your phone for every alert we issue - it is designed as a 'bell ringer' to get your attention when something REALLY bad is headed your way. Will drop a link and screenshots in the comments Most smartphones made in the last 5 or so years should *only* receive WEAs if you are in or very close to the area being warned. If you're on the other side of the county, or in a different county, from a Tornado Warning, for example, you should NOT receive a warning (though older phones may still alert for an entire county).
